rv.q: It’s hard to work out, then, why this production is so bafflingly misjudged.
The difference is that Nero, for all its best intentions, really isn’t ready for prime time, whereas Spring Awakening even at first viewing seemed an instant classic.
Structurally unsound, the show needs significant reworking to fashion it into something more coherent.

After killing his stepfather, Agrippina decides to put her own teenage son Nero on the throne in place of the heir Britannicus, using his epilepsy as an excuse. Certain a time of great influence and power has arrived for her, Agrippina is soon surprised when Nero starts to defy her, killing off his enemies and refusing to be controlled.
Nero is a new musical that takes one of history’s most infamous figures and gives his story a fresh, contemporary twist.
Its biggest obstacle is discovering its own identity, as right now it veers between two completely different tones that don’t complement each other at all, instead resulting in an uneven watch.
Ultimately, Nero can’t decide whether it is a biting political satire, a psychological tragedy, a crude vaudeville comedy or a no-holds-barred rock musical.
Whatever the answer may be, it surely cannot be Nero: A New Musical.
The score may lay itself open to accusations of being a bit of a jumble, but it is the saving grace.

The new musical, whose conception started back in 2003, explores the life of Rome’s most infamous emperor and you would be forgiven for thinking that his exciting life of excess, ambition, cruelty and family drama would make for great theatre. Unfortunately, the show fails to deliver all the way.

cn.t: Despite a talented cast and some strong songs from the Spring Awakening team, this long-gestating musical emerges as a tonally confused, muddled mess that fails to balance its political satire with melodrama.
